newsitem.title: FRANCE: More Algerians slaughtered ahead of Zeroual speech.
newsitem.headline: More Algerians slaughtered ahead of Zeroual speech.

text.p: Algerian residents said on Friday suspected Moslem rebels slew 15 civilians, including 10 women, overnight, only hours before President Liamine Zeroual was due to address the nation on television.
"They were killed on a farm at Ali Baba during the night but it's not clear at what time exactly," one resident said.
The victims were all from one family. Residents nearby said two others, both men, escaped, badly wounded. Some of those killed were also mutilated, one resident said.

There was nono official statement on the slaughter, nor of an unconfirmed report that 22 civilians had been slaughtered over Wednesday-Thursday night. Algeria's tightly controlled radio and television have kept complete silence.

Other residents said six people had been killed in Algiers in the past two nights, including the government-appointed deputy mayor of Badjarrah suburb. He was shot around 8 p.m. on Thursday, said one source.
Algerians have harshly criticised official statements that only "residual terrorism" remained and most had been crushed.
Since the start of Ramadan on January 10, bombs and attacks have killed more than 200 people in and around the capital.

Diplomatic sources in Algiers expect Zeroual -- whose address is scheduled for 8 p.m. (1900 GMT) on Friday -- to speak either of the intensified killings, which the authorities blame on fundamentalists, or on a promised general election, or both.
"Zeroual sees elections as a way out of the violence, but the GIA (Armed Islamic Group) has promised its warby towns.

"The last public statement about a week ago said the state would do its utmost to vanquish terrorism," said one political commentator on Friday, pointing out that the authorities had now stopped referring to 'residual terrorism'.

"No indication has filtered out on the details of his (Zeroual's) speech," Algerian radio said, but added that a special meeting of the unelected National Transitional Council (CNT), a quasi-parliament, would be held on Saturday.
The CNT has been looking at two new laws, one on political parties which particularly bans those based on religion, and one on a system of proportional representation for the poll.
The CNT was set up months after the elected parliament was dissolved by outgoing president Chadli Benjedid early in 1992.
Shortly after, the authorities scrapped an election which the now banned Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) was poised to win.
Around a dozen CNT members have been killed.

State radio said on Friday Zeroual will soon start talks with political parties ahead of elections, seen as a way of bringing the country's 29 million people out of five years of bloodshed. About 60,000 people have died.
But he wants new rules for the poll he has promised in the first half of 1997, with regional elections also this year.
The government-run newspaper El Moudjahid said early this month that the general election would be held in May.
"It's likely to be May 29, with a second round on June 5," one political commentator in Algiers said on Friday.

Diplomats have said Zeroual is determined to ensure there is no repeat of an Islamists' ballot victory. Some believe an election will do little to change events in Algeria other than to give greater legitimacy abroad to the authorities.

"When we had the presidential election, then the referendum on the constitution last year, people expected change. There has been little. I can't see elections altering anything quickly," one diplomatic source said earlier this week.
